paper_title: TARSphere: A Robot-Oriented Full-Stack Framework for Long-Horizon Embodied Agents in Evolving Physical and Social Environments

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Robots must act under physical and social constraints while adapting to changes in their environment and human needs. Existing embodied-agent systems often focus on specified goals or abstract execution into symbolic actions, limiting evaluation in an evolving world. We introduce TARSphere, a robot-oriented full-stack framework for physically and socially grounded long-horizon embodied agents. TARSphere-Infra runs robot policies in a physics simulator with embodied NPCs and constrained dialogue. An event-driven finite-state machine (FSM) uses completed actions and delivered information to update task states and evaluate outcomes. TARSphere-Harness, its embodied brain harness, lets a frozen multimodal large language model (MLLM) act through multi-level executable skills, using observations, hierarchical memory, and execution feedback to revise its decisions. On this foundation, agent-in-the-loop curation aligns task semantics, causal dependencies, and scene geometry to construct TARSphere-Bench: 360 episodes across 30 indoor scenes. Five paired conditions assess perceptual robustness, disruption adaptation, task update, human coordination, and intent understanding for navigate-and-report and fetch-and-deliver tasks. Our evaluation of 8 MLLMs shows that general-purpose models can outperform embodied models, while task updates and human interaction remain difficult. Frequent collisions and falls further motivate evaluating execution safety alongside task success, even with a shared action interface and decision budget.

sections.title:
1 Introduction
Robots operating in everyday environments must account for physical constraints [11], human safety, appro-
priate interaction, and social norms [19, 23]. As the world evolves, sensory conditions, physical access, and
people’s actions and needs can change during execution [8, 9, 23]. Long-horizon tasks therefore require tracking
world states, interpreting human intentions, and adjusting plans using execution feedback [4, 8, 34] (Figure 1).
sections.content: Vision-language-action (VLA) models [3, 10] and world-action models (WAMs) [38] have advanced robot control, yet they often lack the ability to adapt to dynamic and uncertain environments. Large language models (LLMs) provide broad knowledge for reasoning yet lack the ability to perform complex, real-world tasks [1, 8, 9]. This complementarity motivates embodied agents that connect reasoning to action [1, 8, 14, 37]. However, Harness VLA [39], RoboClaw [13], and HumanCLAW [14] focus on tasks with specified goals, leaving an evolving world with human involvement largely unexamined. Other settings, including EmbodiedBenchs high-level tasks [37], LoTa-Bench [5], ALFWorlds text environments [28], and Embodied Agent Interface [12], abstract physical execution into discrete symbolic actions. GRBench [35] combines robot execution with virtual NPC dialogue, while PARTNR [4] evaluates embodied human-robot collaboration with temporal task constraints. These gaps motivate physically and socially grounded foundation for benchmarking robotic agents in an evolving world, with task outcomes tied to execution and human interaction. Insight. Studying embodied intelligence requires physically and socially grounded execution and tasks revealing capabilities across varied situations in changing world (Sections 4.2, 4.3.2 and 4.3.4). Challenge 1: Embodied execution is not symbolic [Sections 4.2 and 4.3.4]. valid action call does not guarantee successful execution: the robot must contend with contact, friction, balance, and human responses. The agent must therefore revise decisions using physical execution feedback. Challenge 2: The world changes during execution [Sections 4.3.2 and 4.3.3]. Physical conditions, human activity, and task requirements can change while plan unfolds. The agent must interpret the current situation and reconsider what to do next. Challenge 3: Evaluation must assess diverse capabilities [Section 4.2]. Within this setting, evaluation must reveal how agents handle varied situations across multiple capability dimensions. Aggregate success alone can mask different capability gaps across task families (Section 4.2). We introduce TARSphere, robot-oriented full-stack framework for embodied agents under physical and social constraints. TARSphere-Infra couples robot controllers with embodied NPCs in physics simulator (Challenge 1). An event-driven FSM maintains world and task states, while TARSphere-Harness combines observations, memory, skills, and execution feedback for replanning (Challenge 2). We build TARSphere-Bench through agent-in-the-loop curation, pairing navigate-and-report and fetch-and-deliver tasks with five capability conditions: perceptual robustness, disruption adaptation, task update, human coordination, and intent understanding (Challenge 3). Paired variants retain their Base scene and task family. Across 8 MLLMs, general-purpose models can outperform embodied models, with capability gaps varying by task family (Section 4.2). Planning credit does not ensure successful execution, and collisions and falls remain common (Sections 4.2 and 4.3.4). These findings call for agents that combine general reasoning, adaptation to world changes, and safe execution (Sections 4.2 and 4.3.2). Our contributions are three-fold. We formulate long-horizon embodied tasks under physical and social constraints, where execution outcomes and world changes continually shape the agents decisions. We develop TARSphere Framework, where physical execution and interaction with embodied humans update task states and supply evaluation evidence; an embodied brain harness uses observations, memory, executable skills, and world feedback to guide model decisions. We introduce agent-in-the-loop curation for 360 TARSphere-Bench episodes in 30 scenes and five paired capability conditions, aligning task semantics, geometry, and execution.

sections.title:
3.1 Problem Formulation
We study physically and socially grounded long-horizon embodied execution in a changing simulated world.
The agent interprets human intent from egocentric observations, communication, and interaction history,
then pursues the required physical outcome or accurate report.

Actions execute sequentially; new observations and feedback inform the next decision. TARSphere Framework implements this loop; TARSphere-Bench supplies tasks and controlled capability conditions there. 3 Figure 2 TARSphere-Infra: execution infrastructure. (a) Physics runtime executes robot actions under contact and friction. (b) An event-driven FSM coordinates NPC actions, message delivery, and task-state transitions. (c) Evaluation checks execution evidence against the task requirements active when that evidence was produced.

sections.title:
3.2.1 TARSphere-Infra
In Figure 2, the harness sends robot actions to a shared execution
Simulation and robot execution.
environment containing G1, task objects, and NPCs in GRScenes-100 [35] scenes. Isaac Sim [21] and PhysX
execute robot control under contact and friction: locomotion follows a learned policy, while grasping executes
planned arm motion and requires physical object acquisition and retention (Section 4.3.4). Episode reset
and synchronization keep sensing, robot control, and NPC motion consistent. Kinematic motion and skeletal
animation keep NPCs’ visible poses aligned with their collision proxies, so visible human motion and robot
contact refer to the same embodied person throughout execution and interaction.
sections.content: Embodied NPCs and constrained dialogue. The NPC runtime maintains each persons pose, behavior, availability, and authorized knowledge. Its LLM backend routes natural questions to authorized topics and returns episode-defined replies. Robot-to-NPC queries require proximity and visibility; NPC speech reaches the robot only within hearing range, so available information depends on the current spatial configuration. Event-driven task state machine. The FSM (Figure 2) tracks event and NPC action status and active task bindings. It admits events when DAG prerequisites and live physical and interaction conditions hold; NPC actions follow IdleQueuedActingDone. Confirmed action completion and actual message delivery commit state transitions, applying authorized updates and enabling dependent stages. The evaluator scores five dependency-checked outcomes against the applicable requirements; task-update events are unscored. fixed semantic judge scores plans and reports; handover requires physical execution and recipient acceptance. We compare semantic scores with human judgments (Section 4.4) and trace responses to task updates through message delivery, goal revision, and physical completion (Sections 4.3.2 and 4.3.3).

sections.title:
3.2.2 Embodied Brain Harness
Closed-loop agent–world interaction. Execution outcomes and world changes can invalidate a plan
(Sections 4.3.2 and 4.3.3). TARSphere-Harness executes actions serially and can return control at tool
boundaries, canceling the remaining actions. Each decision receives current egocentric RGB, body-frame
LiDAR, public events, and execution feedback through Figure 3(a, f). Motion residuals and collision bearings
report movement error and contact direction for subsequent decisions. We ablate motion residuals and LiDAR
observations to examine their contributions to replanning and task completion (Section 4.3.1).
sections.content: Multimodal context and hierarchical memory. As views and task requirements change, TARSphere-Harness retains context through current observations and the memory layers in Figure 3(a, b), whose contributions we examine through ablations (Section 4.3.1). Short-term history retains recent actions, outcomes, and visual4 Figure 3 TARSphere-Harness: the embodied brain harness. (a) Current observations and (b) hierarchical memory inform (c) MLLM decisions. (d) The unified skill interface routes actions to (e) controller backends. (f) Observations, execution feedback, and public world events close the loop. state notes; long-term records retain the active plan, dialogue, and robot state. Semantic spatial memory grounds model-selected people, objects, and places in synchronized RGB-D, storing measured locations and supporting keyframes alongside the online geometric map. Self-managed key memory lets the model retain, revise, or forget selected facts during execution. Unified multi-level skill interface. Through the interface in Figure 3(d), the model combines bounded primitives for body, gaze, and end-effector motion; manipulation skills for locating and grasping visible targets; and navigation skills for reaching points, visual frontiers, or remembered entities using the online map. Social actions use the same interface with spatial preconditions. The controller backends in Figure 3(e) can be replaced by vision-language navigation and action policies. We ablate navigation and grasp skills and separately assess execution accuracy (Sections 4.3.1 and 4.3.4).

sections.title:
3.3 TARSphere-Bench
Task Design and Benchmark Taxonomy. We construct 360 TARSphere-Bench episodes for navigate-and-
report and fetch-and-deliver in 30 GRScenes-100 [35] scenes: 10 homes and 20 commercial spaces. Each
Base episode has five paired conditions sharing its scene, task family, and five-stage evaluation. We test
perceptual robustness (PR) through sensing changes and disruption adaptation (DA) through temporary
blockage or person/tool unavailability while the goal remains fixed. For task update (TU), an authorized
event revises the task; human coordination (HC) requires another person’s information or onsite work, and
intent understanding (IU) requires clarification or contextual inference. HC seeks help toward a known goal;
IU resolves what the person wants. Base comparisons quantify each condition’s effects (Section 4.2).
sections.content: Agent-in-the-Loop Curation. Executable task construction is challenging because semantics, causal dependencies, and scene geometry must agree. Figure 4 outlines four steps. (a) Asset Inputs. Task cards, NPC profiles, and scene assets specify intent, authorized NPC knowledge, and candidate objects and locations. (b) Code-as-Curator Synthesis and Joint Solving. coding agent follows SKILL.md to jointly solve entity bindings, event dependencies, and interaction positions, producing specifications that align task semantics and state transitions with scene geometry. (c) Multi-agent Review and Human Audit. Specialized agents check causality, dialogue, outcome bindings, scoring shortcuts, geometry, and diversity. Human reviewers 5 Figure 4 Agent-in-the-loop curation of TARSphere-Bench. (a) Task, NPC, and scene inputs. (b) Code-as-curator synthesis with joint semantic, causal, and spatial solving. (c) Agent and human review with SKILL.md refinement. (d) Simulation validation of task transitions and execution. assess meaning, naturalness, and layout; critiques guide episode corrections and SKILL.md refinement. (d) Simulation Validation. Simulation checks event delivery and physical execution. We ablate review, curator refinement, and simulation (Section 4.3.5); human evaluation assesses causal soundness and feasibility (Section 4.4). Figure 5 summarizes task and interaction statistics.

sections.title:
4.1 Experimental Setup
We evaluate 8 frozen MLLMs: four proprietary models, GPT-5.6-Terra, Claude Sonnet-5, Gemini-3.8-Flash,
and Qwen3.7-Plus; two general-purpose open VLMs, Qwen3.8-27B [25] and Gemma-4-31B [32]; and two open
embodied models, Hy-Embodied-VLM-1.0 [36] and RoboBrain2.0-32B [31]. All use TARSphere-Harness on
TARSphere-Bench’s 360 episodes, sharing prompts, observations, actions, a 100-decision cap, and termination
rules. By default, decisions use the current image and 10 text-history steps to propose 1-5 actions. All
model weights remain frozen, allowing comparisons through the same harness without benchmark-specific
training, parameter updates, or adaptation to the evaluation tasks.
sections.content: Evaluation Metrics. We use quality scoring for the main results and ablations. The five stages are task understanding, onsite target observation, onsite task completion, recipient observation, and final task completion. The onsite outcome is an inspection conclusion, an answer received from source, or physical grasp, depending on the task. For episode e, let ge,i {0, 1} indicate eligible evidence for stage under its event dependencies and live conditions, and let qe,i [0, 1] score that evidence. sections.title:
4.2 Main Results
(1) Proprietary models lead; the best open VLM outperforms embodied models. In Table 2, Gemini-3.8-
Flash achieves 40.6% navigation and 47.8% delivery success, compared with 16.9% and 24.6% for runner-up
Claude Sonnet-5. Under the shared TARSphere-Harness, proprietary models occupy the top two ranks in both
task families. This lead suggests that broad multimodal competence may be critical for general embodied tasks.
Among open models, Gemma-4-31B succeeds in both families, while both embodied models have low progress
and complete no episodes. The stage breakdown in Figure 6 shows that planning credit does not ensure target
observation or onsite execution. These results motivate preserving multimodal abilities in embodied foundation
model training and testing transfer across diverse tasks and human interactions.

Mechanism ablations. (1) All six removals lower average Progress and Success. Progress falls from 70.5%
to 51.0-67.7%, and Success from 45.8% to 20.8-41.7% (Table 3). Removing LiDAR and motion residuals

25.0 points. (2) Local gains remain condition-specific. Removing semantic spatial memory raises both PR and
HC Success from 41.7% to 58.3%, but lowers average Progress and Success to 67.7% and 41.7%. All variants

The overall pattern supports combining perception, memory, and executable skills for task completion. Configuration trade-offs. (1) Configuration changes yield local gains. Varying text history, image history, and actions per decision improves some metrics and conditions. Two historical images improve Base Success from 58.3% to 66.7%, but average Progress falls from 70.5% to 69.2% and average Success to 38.9%, while mean decisions increase from 43.2 to 47.0. Removing text history reduces tokens per decision from 10.5k to 9.9k, yet requires 47.4 decisions and lowers Success to 36.1%. Four historical images reduce decisions to 41.3, with lower Success of 37.5%. Longer text history and fixed threeor five-action horizons also use more tokens per decision without improving average Success. (2) The default balances performance and cost: ten text steps, the current image, and adaptive one-to-five-action decisions achieve the highest tested average Progress and Success at 43.2 decisions and 10.5k tokens per decision.

Egocentric views, reasoning excerpts, and event-triggered causal milestones contrast successful reporting, recovery failure, wrong-person interaction, and unsupported completion claims. Execution gains do not imply smaller capability gaps. sections.title:
5 Conclusion
TARSphere grounds long-horizon robot tasks in shared physical and social constraints (Sections 4.2 and 4.3.4).
TARSphere Framework couples robot dynamics, embodied NPC interaction, and state-machine control and
evaluation; TARSphere-Harness lets frozen MLLMs act through memory, executable skills, and measured
feedback (Sections 4.3.1 and 4.4). TARSphere-Bench pairs two service task families with five capability
demands, supporting trajectory-based comparisons of model decisions, completion, and execution quality as
demands change during execution, including revised goals and dependencies on human participation.
sections.content: Limitations and Future Work. We evaluate one robot body and two indoor service task families in simulation. Real-robot transfer must address differences in sensing, contact, and human behavior. We plan Mobile-Franka transfer and task-adapted VLA, navigation, and manipulation backends.
